prelim.title.label: Title Page
prelim.title.guideline:
State the name of the system, its type/platform (web-based, mobile, desktop), its purpose, and the locale or users.
Pattern: [SYSTEM NAME]: A [Platform] [Type of System] for [Users/Office] of [Locale].
Example: LabTrack: A Web-Based Laboratory Equipment Inventory and Borrowing System for the Science Department of Cabiao Senior High School.
Keep it within about 20 words, typed in ALL CAPS and bold, arranged in an inverted pyramid on the title page.

suggest.title: Suggest 3 research titles of about 20 words following the pattern SYSTEM NAME: A Platform Type of System for Users of Locale.

prelim.acknowledgment.label: Acknowledgment
prelim.acknowledgment.guideline:
Optional but customary. Keep it to one page.
Thank, in order: your research adviser and panel, the school head, the office or users who allowed you to study their process, the IT experts and end-users who evaluated the system, and your families.
Keep the tone formal and sincere. Avoid nicknames, jokes, and long personal stories.
prelim.acknowledgment.rules: One page or less. Formal and sincere. Order: adviser and panel, school head, office or users, IT experts and end-users, families. Thank only those listed in INPUT.

prelim.abstract.label: Abstract
prelim.abstract.guideline:
One paragraph, 150–250 words, past tense, with no citations, tables, or abbreviations that are not explained.
Include, in order: (1) the problem and purpose of the study; (2) the research design and software development model used; (3) the tools and technologies used; (4) the respondents and instrument (ISO/IEC 25010); (5) key results, such as the overall weighted mean and its interpretation; and (6) the main conclusion and recommendation.
Write it last, after Chapters 1–5 are final.
prelim.abstract.rules: One paragraph only, 150 to 250 words, no citations and no tables. Cover the problem, design and model, tools, respondents and instrument, key results, and conclusion. Use only results that appear in INPUT.context.

suggest.keywords: Suggest 5 keywords, each one short, drawn from the system and the study.

ch1.background.label: Background
ch1.background.guideline:
Explain why the system is needed. Move from the general situation to your specific locale and problem. Suggested flow (one or more paragraphs each):
Context. The problem area and the role of technology or information systems in it, globally and in the Philippines. Support with cited sources.
Current situation at the locale. How the process is done now (manual, spreadsheet, or old system), who does it, and how often. Use evidence from interviews, observation, or records, such as the number of transactions or time spent.
Problems encountered. Specific difficulties: delays, errors, lost records, duplicate entries, slow report generation, lack of security.
Gap. Why existing solutions do not fully address the problem at your locale.
Proposed solution. The system you will develop, what it will do, and who will benefit. State how the study aligns with your class research agenda and the DepEd Basic Education Research Agenda (DepEd Order No. 39, s. 2016).
Length: 2–3 pages. Do not start with dictionary definitions. Avoid one-sentence paragraphs.
ch1.background.rules: Use the student's answers in INPUT.inputs.answers and any notes in the other inputs. Where a required fact about the locale is still unknown, write a short gap such as [KULANG: weekly transactions] instead of guessing. Refer to people at the locale by their role, such as the laboratory custodian, and never by name. Flow: context, current situation, problems, gap, proposed solution, alignment with the class research agenda and DepEd Order No. 39, s. 2016. Do not open with a dictionary definition. No one-sentence paragraphs. Every outside claim needs a citation from INPUT.sources. Use only the evidence the student gave.

ch1.sop.label: Statement of the Problem
ch1.sop.guideline:
Begin with the general problem: “This study aims to design, develop, and evaluate [system name], a [platform] [type of system] for [users] of [locale].”
Follow with specific research questions that are clear, measurable, and answerable by your data. Each question will have its own section in Chapter 4, in the same order.
Avoid yes-or-no questions except for the hypothesis-testing question. Adjust the sample questions below to your study.

suggest.questions: Suggest 3 additional research questions that fit a system development study and follow the template's style.

ch1.objectives.label: Objectives
ch1.objectives.guideline:
This part is added for system development studies. It restates each research question as a specific objective that starts with an action verb: identify, determine, design, develop, test, evaluate, compare, propose.
Write one general objective, then specific objectives that match the Statement of the Problem one-to-one.
ch1.objectives.rules: First a paragraph stating the general objective: to design, develop, and evaluate the system. Then one list with exactly one specific objective for each research question in INPUT.context, in the same order, each starting with an action verb.

suggest.objectives: Suggest one specific objective for a research question that has none yet, starting with an action verb.

ch1.framework.label: Conceptual Framework
ch1.framework.guideline:
Use the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model, the usual framework for system development studies.
Input: knowledge requirements (problems in the current process, user requirements, related literature and systems), software requirements (programming language, framework, database), and hardware requirements.
Process: the phases of your chosen software development model (such as planning, analysis, design, development, testing, and deployment) and the evaluation using ISO/IEC 25010.
Output: the developed and evaluated [System Name]. You may add a feedback arrow from Output back to Input to show iteration.
Draw the diagram with shapes in Word, draw.io, or Canva, then explain each box in one or two paragraphs. The Process box must match the methodology in Chapter 3.
ch1.framework.rules: Explain the Input-Process-Output framework in paragraphs. The Process must match the development phases named by the student. Do not draw the diagram.

ch1.scope.label: Scope and Limitations
ch1.scope.guideline:
Scope: what the system covers, including its modules and features, user roles (administrator, staff, student), platform (web, Android, desktop), locale, respondents, and school year (S.Y. 2026–2027).
Limitations: what the system will not do, such as no online payment, local network only, or no SMS notifications. Include constraints such as the number of respondents, devices used in testing, internet connectivity, and the fact that long-term use was not measured.
Be specific. The panel will check whether your output matches what you promised here.
ch1.scope.rules: Two organized parts: what the study covers, then its limitations. Be specific about modules, roles, platform, locale, respondents, and school year. The panel checks the finished system against this.

suggest.limits: Suggest 3 realistic limitations for this kind of system, such as features or settings it will not cover.

ch1.significance.label: Significance
ch1.significance.guideline:
This part is the CG’s Importance of the Study. Name each beneficiary in bold, followed by how the system or study will specifically help them.
Order the beneficiaries from most to least direct: end-users (students, teachers, staff), the office or school administration, the researchers, ICT/TVL learners, and future researchers.
Write one paragraph for each beneficiary. Avoid generic statements such as “this study will help them a lot.”
ch1.significance.rules: One paragraph per beneficiary row, in the given order. Put the beneficiary's name in lead exactly as given, and do not split, rename, or add beneficiaries. Put the benefit in text. No generic claims. Use the specific benefit the student wrote.

ch1.terms.label: Definition of Terms
ch1.terms.guideline:
Define the key terms in your title, research questions, and system, including technical terms such as module, database, framework, user acceptance testing, and ISO/IEC 25010.
Arrange terms alphabetically. Give the operational definition, meaning how the term is used in your study. Add a conceptual definition with a citation if helpful.
Format: the term in bold followed by a period, then the definition in one to three sentences.
ch1.terms.rules: One paragraph for each term in INPUT and no others, alphabetical. Put the term in lead and an operational definition of 1 to 3 sentences in text, stating how the term is used in this study.

suggest.terms: Suggest 5 technical terms from this study that readers may need defined. Give only the terms.

ch2.literature.label: Related Literature
ch2.literature.guideline:
Discuss concepts, theories, and technologies found in books, articles, and documentation. Use subheadings for each topic, for example:
(a) the problem domain (such as inventory management or attendance monitoring); (b) information systems in schools or organizations; (c) the technologies you will use (programming language, framework, database); (d) your software development model; and (e) software quality and ISO/IEC 25010.
ch2.literature.rules: Use INPUT.inputs.research_topics as the themes, with one heading3 per topic. Use only what each source's notes say. Organize by theme with one heading3 per topic, using the student's topics. Every claim traces to a citation from INPUT.sources. Synthesize sources instead of summarizing them one by one.
ch2.literature.topics_rule: Recommend 3 to 5 review topics that the study's literature must cover, drawn from the approved Chapter 1.

ch2.studies.label: Related Studies
ch2.studies.guideline:
Review previous research, such as theses and journal articles, that developed or evaluated similar systems.
For each study, give the author and year, purpose, method (development model, respondents, instrument), key findings, and its relation to your study (similarities and differences).
ch2.studies.rules: Use heading3 'Foreign Studies' and heading3 'Local Studies', using each source's origin in INPUT.sources. For each study give its purpose, method, findings, and relation to this study, stating only what its notes say and leaving out what they do not.
ch2.studies.topics_rule: Recommend 2 to 3 focused research areas for finding studies similar to this one, drawn from the approved Chapter 1.

ch2.systems.label: Related Systems
ch2.systems.guideline:
This part is added for system development studies. Describe 3–5 existing systems or applications (commercial, open-source, or developed in other studies) that do something similar to your proposed system.
For each, give a short description, its main features, its strengths, and its limitations. You may include a screenshot with a proper source citation.
ch2.systems.rules: One paragraph per comparable system described in INPUT.sources, 3 to 5 in all. Put the system's name or a short description of it in lead. State its features and strengths only as its notes report them, and leave out what they do not say. Add to missing_info that the students should try the actual systems and add what they observe.
ch2.systems.topics_rule: Recommend 2 to 3 search areas for finding published descriptions of existing systems comparable to this one, drawn from the approved Chapter 1.

ch2.synthesis.label: Synthesis and Gap
ch2.synthesis.guideline:
Summarize the common findings of the literature, studies, and systems you reviewed. Then state clearly the gap: what is still missing and how your system addresses it.
Support the synthesis with a feature comparison matrix, such as the sample table below. Write Yes or No in each cell, then discuss the table in a paragraph.
ch2.synthesis.rules: State common findings, the gap, and how the proposed system fills it. Mention the comparison table using its reference token. The discussion must agree with the Yes and No values in the table.

ch3.design.label: Research Design
ch3.design.guideline:
Name the design and define it with a citation. Most system development studies use the developmental research design (designing, developing, and evaluating a product), combined with a descriptive quantitative design to describe the evaluation results.
Explain why this design fits your study in one paragraph.
ch3.design.rules: State the research design, its source, and why it fits. Cite only from INPUT.sources. Write up the design named in INPUT.choice for this study and explain why it fits, citing only INPUT.sources.
ch3.design.options_rule: Recommend 3 research designs suited to this system development study, such as developmental, descriptive quantitative, or mixed methods.

ch3.method.overview.label: Methodology Overview
ch3.method.overview.guideline:
Name the software development model you used, such as Agile (Scrum), Waterfall, Rapid Application Development (RAD), Prototyping, Iterative and Incremental, or V-Model. Cite its source and present its diagram as a figure.
Justify your choice. For example, Agile suits projects where user feedback is gathered repeatedly; Waterfall suits projects with fixed, well-defined requirements.
Discuss each phase under its own subheading. Rename, add, or merge the sample phases below to match your model. For each phase, state what was done, who was involved, the tools used, and the output of the phase.
ch3.method.overview.rules: Explain the software development model, its source, why it was chosen, and its phases. Explain the software development model named in INPUT.facts.dev_model, why it suits this study. Then name each of these phases and describe its main activities under this model: Requirements Planning and Analysis, System Design, Development, Testing, and Deployment and Evaluation. Write 2 to 3 sentences on each phase from general knowledge of the model. Use no [KULANG] gaps in this part.

ch3.method.phase1.label: Phase 1 Requirements
ch3.method.phase1.guideline:
Describe how you gathered requirements: interviews with the office head or users, observation of the current process, and review of forms and records. Put your interview guide in Appendix E.
Present the functional requirements (“The system shall allow the administrator to…”) and non-functional requirements (speed, security, ease of use). List the user roles and what each role can do.
ch3.method.phase1.rules: Describe the requirements activities the student listed, then functional and non-functional requirements and user roles. Mention the interview guide using {{ref:appendix:interview}} only if interviews were done. Describe the usual activities of this phase under the development model. Use the system's modules and users from INPUT.facts. Mark anything specific to this project that INPUT does not state, such as tools, versions, or names of documents, with a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch3.method.phase2.label: Phase 2 Design
ch3.method.phase2.guideline:
Describe how the system was designed and the tools used (draw.io, Figma, Canva). Design outputs include the system architecture, use case diagram or data flow diagram (context diagram and level 0), entity relationship diagram (ERD), system flowchart, and user interface wireframes or mockups.
To avoid repetition, describe the design activities here and present the final diagrams as results in Chapter 4, which answers the research question on design and development. Follow your adviser if they prefer the diagrams here.
ch3.method.phase2.rules: Describe design activities and tools. The diagrams appear in Chapter 4, so do not describe their contents. Describe the usual activities of this phase under the development model. Use the system's modules and users from INPUT.facts. Mark anything specific to this project that INPUT does not state, such as tools, versions, or names of documents, with a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch3.method.phase3.label: Phase 3 Development
ch3.method.phase3.guideline:
Describe how the system was built: the programming languages, frameworks, database management system, integrated development environment (IDE), and version control (such as Git and GitHub).
Explain the order in which the modules were built (per sprint or iteration, if Agile), coding conventions followed, and any open-source libraries used, with proper credit.
Disclose any use of AI coding assistants here, following your school’s policy.
ch3.method.phase3.rules: Describe languages, frameworks, database, IDE, version control, and build order exactly as given, with any versions. Include any AI assistance the student disclosed. Describe the usual activities of this phase under the development model. Use the system's modules and users from INPUT.facts. Mark anything specific to this project that INPUT does not state, such as tools, versions, or names of documents, with a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch3.method.phase4.label: Phase 4 Testing
ch3.method.phase4.guideline:
Describe the levels of testing done: unit testing (each function or module), integration testing (modules working together), system testing (the whole system), and user acceptance testing (UAT) with actual users.
Explain how test cases were prepared and how bugs were recorded and fixed. Present the results in Chapter 4 and the complete test cases in Appendix F.
ch3.method.phase4.rules: Describe testing levels, how test cases were made, and how bugs were handled. Refer to the full list using {{ref:appendix:test_cases}}. Describe the usual activities of this phase under the development model. Use the system's modules and users from INPUT.facts. Mark anything specific to this project that INPUT does not state, such as tools, versions, or names of documents, with a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch3.method.phase5.label: Phase 5 Deployment
ch3.method.phase5.guideline:
Describe how the system was installed or hosted at the locale (local server, school computer, web hosting, APK installation), how users were oriented, and how the user manual (Appendix H) was used.
Explain that the system was then evaluated by the respondents using the instrument described below.
ch3.method.phase5.rules: Describe how the system was installed, how users were oriented, and how evaluation followed. Refer to the manual using {{ref:appendix:manual}}. Describe the usual activities of this phase under the development model. Use the system's modules and users from INPUT.facts. Mark anything specific to this project that INPUT does not state, such as tools, versions, or names of documents, with a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch3.requirements.label: System Requirements
ch3.requirements.guideline:
Present the hardware and software used to develop the system, and the minimum requirements needed to run it.
Use specific versions, such as “PHP 8.3” or “MySQL 8.0,” not just “PHP” or “MySQL.” Explain the tables briefly in the text.
ch3.requirements.rules: Write a brief explanation that introduces the two tables using their reference tokens. Do not repeat the table rows.

ch3.locale.label: Locale
ch3.locale.guideline: Describe where the system was developed, deployed, and evaluated: the school or office, its location, and the users of the process being improved. You may include a location map as a figure.
ch3.locale.rules: Describe where the system was developed, deployed, and evaluated, using only what the student wrote.

ch3.population.label: Population and Respondents
ch3.population.guideline:
Describe the population and the respondents who will evaluate the system. There are usually two groups:
IT experts, such as ICT teachers, programmers, and IT professionals, who evaluate the technical quality of the system. State their qualifications.
End-users, such as students, teachers, and staff who will actually use the system.
Agree with your adviser on the number of respondents. Present them in a table like the one below.
ch3.population.rules: Describe the population and the two respondent groups and their qualifications. Mention the table using its reference token.

ch3.sampling.label: Sampling
ch3.sampling.guideline:
Name and explain the sampling technique for each group, with a citation. Purposive sampling is commonly used for IT experts, so state the selection criteria. End-users may be chosen by purposive, convenience, or stratified random sampling.
If the end-user population is large, compute the sample size using Slovin’s formula: n = N / (1 + Ne²), where n is the sample size, N is the population, and e is the margin of error (such as 0.05).
ch3.sampling.rules: Describe the technique for each group, selection criteria, and its source. Do not recalculate any sample size. Write up the sampling technique named in INPUT.choice as applied to the respondent groups in INPUT.context. State the selection criteria as a [KULANG: ...] gap if INPUT does not give them. Do not calculate a sample size.

ch3.instrument.label: Research Instrument
ch3.instrument.guideline:
Describe the evaluation questionnaire based on the ISO/IEC 25010 software product quality model, using a 5-point Likert scale. Typical parts: Part I, respondent profile (optional); Part II, evaluation indicators for each quality characteristic (3–5 statements each); and Part III, comments and suggestions. Put the questionnaire in Appendix C.
If you adapted an existing questionnaire, cite its source and ask the author’s permission if possible.
Validity: have the instrument checked by at least three validators, such as an ICT teacher, a research teacher, and a language teacher. Put the validation certificates in Appendix D.
Reliability (optional): pilot-test the instrument and compute Cronbach’s alpha. A value of 0.70 or higher is generally acceptable.
Note: most studies use the eight characteristics of the 2011 edition, shown below. The 2023 edition renamed usability as interaction capability and portability as flexibility, and added safety. Use the version your adviser prefers and cite it.
ch3.instrument.rules: Describe the questionnaire, validation, and reliability using only what the student gave. Mention the ISO/IEC 25010 table using its reference token. Describe the evaluation questionnaire. In rows, give at least 3 and at most 5 separate rating statements for every characteristic in INPUT.tables, so there are at least 24 rows, each specific to this system and its modules, with characteristic spelled exactly as in that table and indicator as one short statement a respondent can rate. Validation details not in INPUT are [KULANG: ...] gaps.

suggest.indicators: Suggest 5 clear evaluation statements for this system that a respondent can rate from 1 to 5.

ch3.gathering.label: Data Gathering
ch3.gathering.guideline: Present the steps in chronological order as a numbered list, from securing permission to analyzing the data. Adjust the sample steps below.
ch3.gathering.rules: One list with the steps in chronological order. Keep every step and every {{ref:...}} token the student has. One list of the data gathering steps in chronological order: permission, requirements gathering, development and testing, instrument validation, informed consent and assent, system demonstration, questionnaire administration, and analysis. Use {{ref:appendix:permission}} and {{ref:appendix:consent}}.

ch3.ethics.label: Ethics
ch3.ethics.guideline:
Explain how you protected the respondents and maintained research integrity: informed consent, parental consent and assent for minors, voluntary participation, and the right to withdraw.
Explain how personal data were kept confidential in compliance with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173). Use dummy data, not real personal records, during development and testing.
State that all sources, open-source code, and libraries were properly credited, and disclose any AI assistance.
ch3.ethics.rules: Must mention the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173), consent and assent, voluntary participation, and the right to withdraw. Describe only what the student says was done. Write the commitments the study follows: informed consent and parental assent for minors, voluntary participation, the right to withdraw, confidentiality under the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173), dummy data during development and testing, and credit for all sources, open-source code, and libraries. Do not write about AI use, because a separate statement covers it.

ch4.problems.label: Current Problems
ch4.problems.guideline: Answers research question 1. Summarize what you found during requirements gathering, then show how each problem is addressed by a feature or module of the system.
ch4.problems.rules: Present only what was actually found. Mention the table using its reference token. Present the problems the students already reported in INPUT.context. In rows, pair each problem with the module of the system that addresses it.

ch4.design.architecture.label: Architecture
ch4.design.architecture.guideline:
Answers research questions 2 and 3. Present the final design and the developed system.
Use clear, cropped screenshots. Number every figure and describe each one in a short paragraph covering what the screen is for, who uses it, and what the user can do.
Do not paste source code here. Put selected code or the repository link in Appendix I.
ch4.design.architecture.rules: Explain how users, interface, server, and database work together. Base this only on INPUT.repository, the students' actual code, and describe what is really there. If something cannot be told from it, use a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch4.design.usecase.label: Use Case or DFD
ch4.design.usecase.guideline:
Answers research questions 2 and 3. Present the final design and the developed system.
Use clear, cropped screenshots. Number every figure and describe each one in a short paragraph covering what the screen is for, who uses it, and what the user can do.
Do not paste source code here. Put selected code or the repository link in Appendix I.
ch4.design.usecase.rules: Explain the users of the system and the processes they perform. Base this only on INPUT.repository, the students' actual code, and describe what is really there. If something cannot be told from it, use a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch4.design.database.label: Database
ch4.design.database.guideline:
Answers research questions 2 and 3. Present the final design and the developed system.
Use clear, cropped screenshots. Number every figure and describe each one in a short paragraph covering what the screen is for, who uses it, and what the user can do.
Do not paste source code here. Put selected code or the repository link in Appendix I.
ch4.design.database.rules: Explain the tables and relationships exactly as the student described them. Base this only on INPUT.repository, the students' actual code, and describe what is really there. If something cannot be told from it, use a [KULANG: ...] gap.

ch4.design.modules.label: Modules and UI
ch4.design.modules.guideline:
Answers research questions 2 and 3. Present the final design and the developed system.
Use clear, cropped screenshots. Number every figure and describe each one in a short paragraph covering what the screen is for, who uses it, and what the user can do.
Do not paste source code here. Put selected code or the repository link in Appendix I.
ch4.design.modules.rules: One paragraph per screen. Put the screen name in lead. State its purpose, who uses it, and what they can do. Describe only what the student wrote. Base this only on INPUT.repository. In rows, give each main screen found in the code, with name as the screen and description as its purpose, who uses it, and what they can do.

ch4.testing.label: System Testing
ch4.testing.guideline:
Summarize the testing results. Report the number of test cases, how many passed, and the pass rate. Show sample test cases in a table and put the complete list in Appendix F.
Mention bugs found and how they were fixed before the evaluation.
ch4.testing.rules: Report the totals from INPUT.tables without changing them. Failed cases must stay visible. Describe bugs and fixes only as the student wrote them. In rows, propose 10 to 15 test cases across the modules, with id such as TC-01, module, scenario, and expected. Never fill in actual results. Discuss the results using only INPUT.tables and INPUT.computed_summary.

ch4.acceptability.label: Acceptability
ch4.acceptability.guideline:
Answers research question 4. Present the summary table of weighted means for each ISO/IEC 25010 characteristic. You may present a detailed table per characteristic (indicator by indicator) before the summary, or place them in the appendix.
Sample interpretation: “Table __ shows that the system was rated Highly Acceptable overall (WM = __). Usability obtained the highest mean (WM = __), which implies that…. This agrees with the findings of (Author, Year), who….”
ch4.acceptability.rules: Follow presentation, analysis, interpretation, and support from related literature. Mention the highest and lowest characteristics, and the overall mean, using only values and verbal interpretations from INPUT.tables. Do not repeat every number. Mention the table using its reference token.

ch4.difference.label: Significant Difference
ch4.difference.guideline: Answers research question 5. Include this only if you stated a hypothesis. Report the test used, the computed value, the p-value, the decision on Ho (reject or fail to reject), and its meaning.
ch4.difference.rules: State the mean, standard deviation, t-value, p-value, and decision on the null hypothesis exactly as in INPUT.tables. Explain what the result means. Mention the table using its reference token.

ch4.enhancements.label: Enhancements
ch4.enhancements.guideline: Answers research question 6. Based on the respondents’ comments and the lowest-rated characteristics, list the enhancements that can improve the system.
ch4.enhancements.rules: Propose only enhancements grounded in the respondents' comments and lowest-rated characteristics given in INPUT. Propose enhancements based on the lowest-rated characteristics in INPUT.context and any respondent comments in INPUT.inputs.text.

ch5.summary.label: Summary of Findings
ch5.summary.guideline:
Begin with a short paragraph restating the purpose, design, and respondents of the study.
List the findings numbered in the same order as the research questions. State the key results and values briefly, such as “The system was rated Highly Acceptable (WM = 4.52).”
Do not add new data or discussion.
ch5.summary.rules: A short paragraph restating the purpose, design, and respondents, then one list with one finding per research question, in order. No new data.

ch5.conclusions.label: Conclusions
ch5.conclusions.guideline:
Give one conclusion for each finding. A conclusion is a generalization that directly answers a research question. It is not a repetition of the numbers.
If you tested a hypothesis, state whether Ho was rejected or not.
ch5.conclusions.rules: One list with one conclusion per finding, in order. Generalize instead of repeating numbers. State the decision on the null hypothesis if it was tested.

ch5.recommendations.label: Recommendations
ch5.recommendations.guideline:
Each recommendation must come from a conclusion. Make them specific and doable, and address them to the beneficiaries named in the Significance of the Study.
Include recommendations for adoption (school or office), for users, and for future researchers, such as features to add (a mobile version, SMS or email notifications, cloud hosting, analytics) and a larger or longer evaluation.
ch5.recommendations.rules: One list. Each recommendation follows from a conclusion and is addressed to a beneficiary named in INPUT.context.

suggest.items: Suggest 3 recommendations that follow from the conclusions, each addressed to a named beneficiary.

app.permission.label: A Permission
app.permission.guideline: The signed letter addressed to the principal or office head asking permission to conduct the study and deploy the system.
app.permission.rules: Polish this letter of permission for adviser review. Keep every {{...}} name and every fact. Leave signature lines to the students. Write a formal letter asking the school head, {{PRINCIPAL}}, for permission to conduct the study, using INPUT.facts. Leave signature lines for the students and adviser.

app.consent.label: B Consent
app.consent.guideline: Blank copies of the consent form for adult respondents, and the parental consent and assent form for respondents below 18 years old.
app.consent.rules: Polish this blank consent and assent form for adviser review. Keep voluntary participation, the right to withdraw, and data privacy under RA 10173. Write a blank informed consent and parental assent form, with blank lines for names and signatures.

app.interview.label: E Interview Guide
app.interview.guideline: The questions used when interviewing the office head or users about the current process (optional).
app.interview.rules: One list of open-ended interview questions that gather the system's requirements.

suggest.items: Suggest 5 open-ended interview questions that gather requirements for this system.

finish.defense.label: Defense Prep
finish.defense.guideline:
Submit the draft written research report for oral presentation (Chapters 1–5, references, and appendices) on or before the date set by your teacher.
Prepare a slide presentation of about 10–15 slides: title; background and problem; objectives; conceptual framework; methodology; live system demonstration; results; and conclusions and recommendations.
Test the system on the actual device and venue. Prepare a backup, such as a screen-recorded demo video and an offline copy, in case of internet or hardware problems.
Every member must understand the whole paper and the system, including the code. Expect questions about how a feature works.
Assign members to present different parts, but answer questions as a group. Answer honestly. If you don’t know, say so and note the question.
Assign one member to write down all comments and suggestions. Your teacher will also document the proceedings.
Revise the paper and the system based on the panel’s suggestions, then fill out the Revision Matrix (Appendix L) for checking and signing.
Submit the final written research report after the revisions are approved.
finish.defense.rules: Make 10 to 15 slides in this order: title; background and problem; objectives; conceptual framework; methodology; live system demonstration; results; conclusions and recommendations. At most 5 short points per slide. Make 10 to 12 questions that a panel is likely to ask about this specific system, its code, its method, and its results.

app.manual.label: H User Manual
app.manual.guideline: Step-by-step instructions, with screenshots, on how to install, log in, and use each module of the system.
app.manual.rules: Turn the student's steps into clear numbered instructions, grouped by module with heading3. Add no feature the student did not describe. Write instructions for installing, logging in, and using each module, based on INPUT.repository and INPUT.context. Add no feature that is not there.

app.validation.label: D Validation
app.validation.guideline: Signed certificates from the validators who checked the questionnaire.
app.validation.rules: Write a blank validation certificate for the research instrument, with blank lines for the validator's name, signature, and date.

app.editing.label: K Editing Certificate
app.editing.guideline: Signed by the English teacher or editor who checked the grammar of the paper (optional).
app.editing.rules: Write a blank certificate of editing, with blank lines for the editor's name, signature, and date.
